entities.summary:
The Alids (Alawids / descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib) are the descendants of the fourth Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib and his wife Fatima (daughter of the Prophet Muhammad) — the lineage from which Shi'a Islam derives its imams and from which dozens of ruling dynasties have claimed legitimacy across 1,400 years of Islamic history. The Alid claim to leadership (based on prophetic descent) versus the Umayyad/Abbasid claim (based on tribal seniority and political power) was the foundational schism of Islam, generating Shi'a theology, the Fatimid Caliphate, the Safavid Empire, and modern Iran.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (c. 600-661 CE) was the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law; his supporters (Shi'at Ali — 'partisans of Ali') contested the first three caliphates as illegitimate, arguing that leadership should pass through Muhammad's family (ahl al-bayt). Ali became the fourth Caliph (656-661 CE) but was assassinated; his son Hasan renounced the caliphate; his son Husayn was killed with 72 companions at Karbala (680 CE) — the foundational trauma of Shi'a Islam, commemorated in Ashura.

Alid dynasties include: Fatimids (909-1171, Tunisia/Egypt — claiming descent through Fatima), Zaydi imamates (still governing Yemen through 1962 and the Houthi movement today), Hasanid dynasties (Morocco's Alawi dynasty claims Hasanid descent), Idrisids of Morocco (788-985 CE), and the Safavids (who claimed Alid descent to legitimize their Shi'a Persian state). The 12 Imams of Twelver Shi'a Islam (the largest Shi'a branch, dominant in Iran, Iraq, and Lebanon) are all Alids — the Twelfth Imam (Muhammad al-Mahdi) is believed to be in occultation since 874 CE, awaiting eschatological return.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Alids — through the Shi'a-Sunni split their legitimacy claim generated — are the ancestral lineage responsible for Islam's most consequential internal division, shaping the Fatimid Caliphate, Safavid Empire, and Islamic Republic of Iran, and making the 680 CE Battle of Karbala the most politically influential martyrdom in world history.
